point: The chapter surveys power system optimisation models similar to EMPIRE across horizons, spatial detail, scope, scenario generation and operational complexity.
Hydropower management is the main focus, so the chapter covers model structure and uncertainty first to make its challenges understandable.
Optimisation models must balance realism against complexity and computation time.
Models covering the same time horizon turn out to be quite similar.
Uncertainty is unavoidable in power system models and more so with variable renewables, but it adds complexity, so treatment depends on model purpose.
Most reviewed models are deterministic, trading away uncertainty for spatial, temporal and technical detail, while EMPIRE uses multi-horizon stochastic programming.
Models are stochastic, deterministic or mixed, and the mostly deterministic choice likely reflects the need to limit complexity in large models.
Regulated hydropower is modelled either as a generator or as storage, depending on the model's detail and focus.
Modelling hydro as storage gives long-term flexibility but, without inflow uncertainty, lets the model adjust production with unrealistic perfect foresight.
One proposed remedy combines inter-period and intra-period variables for seasonal variation, but adds operational complexity.
Treating regulated hydro as unregulated generation avoids complexity but greatly underestimates flexibility, reflecting priority of spatial and temporal detail in long-term models.
Separating regulated and pumped hydro misses flexibility in systems like Norway, while combining them captures it but may add pumping to reservoirs lacking it.
Few models combine inter-period connection with operational uncertainty, and modelling this for hydropower would show its flexibility in renewable-heavy systems.
The main challenge is combining stochasticity with hydropower flexibility without making the model too complex.
